entities.summary:
The Battle of Tannenberg was a pivotal World War I engagement between German and Russian forces, taking place in eastern Poland on August 23-30, 1914. 

 The German Eighth Army, led by General Paul von Hindenburg and Ludwig von Falkenhausen, decisively defeated the Russian Second Army, led by General Alexander Samsonov, in a four-day battle that saw the Russians suffer heavy casualties and equipment losses. 

 This crushing defeat marked a significant turning point on the Eastern Front, as the Germans continued their advance into Russia, eventually reaching the outskirts of Warsaw. 

 The battle's strategic importance cannot be overstated, as it not only halted the Russian invasion of East Prussia but also set the stage for Germany's subsequent victories on the Eastern Front, including the capture of Vilna and the advance on the Dvina River. 

 At the same time, the battle had far-reaching consequences for Russia, which would struggle to recover from the losses incurred at Tannenberg for the remainder of the war and beyond.

 The Battle of Tannenberg is often regarded as one of the greatest battles of World War I, with the German forces' use of infiltration tactics and the effective employment of machine guns and artillery being key factors in their ultimate victory.
